utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to continue the cross-examination of Witness DP34?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we then perhaps first have the curtains pulled down. And then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Your Honour, I just wanted to add something about the document that your assistant that is provide you with. That's page 2 of document 1453. The Defence has provided the interpreters with a sufficient number of copies. And if a translation is necessary during the break, I can provide it because I have asked for it to be translated. If this is necessary, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if there would be a translation, then at least we can have a global knowledge of what the content is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Mundis, please proceed -- yes. Is there anything you'd like to ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a request, Your Honour. I've been told that these hearings are relayed to Yugoslavia, B92. I think that's the name. I would once again like to request, since this voice is known -- I would like to request that we go into private session when we mention names, when the Prosecutor asks questions about the names of people. You know what happens over there. Murders are committed of high-ranking police officials, and I quite simply feel at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. As you may have noticed yesterday, when you asked to go into private session when you mentioned names, we granted that you would give these answers in private session, of course. But if names are mentioned by one of the parties, of course I cannot prevent that. It's your testimony that we can take measures. But perhaps we could -- the Chamber could invite the parties then whenever questions are put in respect of where you could expect names of higher-ranking officials to be part of the answer, that perhaps the question already would be put in private session. So I invited the parties also to put -- if questions are put which one could expect that would result in an answer giving names, that already that question would be put in private session as well. Yes. You had some -- you wanted to ask anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said high-ranking officials. But no, even the names of ordinary persons. These people, the most dangerous person, criminals, et cetera, that's what I was thinking of. When names are mentioned, it doesn't matter whether someone has an official position or had no position whatsoever. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Whenever there's any need, please tell us and we'll give a decision. Yes, not only high-ranking officials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you had been told that these proceedings were broadcast on B92. Do you recall when you were told this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Friday. On Friday, when the previous witness was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday when we broke we were discussing paramilitaries. Do you know what type of arms any of the paramilitary forces that were operating in the SRK area of responsibility were equipped with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes. I don't know about everything, but I do know something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of weapons did the paramilitaries have that you -- that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the standard weapons that the army and police of the former Yugoslavia had, they had some of these standard weapons, but they also had certain special weapons that the police force did not have. For example, Heckler rifles. Then they had several Motorolas. And this concerned some of them. They had different uniforms, some kind of gloves with openings here, and so on, special footwear. They had some kind of shoes which were lighter than the ones that we used to wear, the former police and the former army. They were of this colour more or less, brown. Those were the light weapons, but they also had heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with -- in an attempt to clarify, let's start with standard weapons. What type of weapons would you consider to be standard weapons that the army and police of the former Yugoslavia had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Standard infantry weapon? Is that what you are thinking of? Rifles, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifle, light machine-guns, mostly produced in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also indicated that they had certain special weapons, including Heckler rifles. What is a Heckler rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a short rifle. They also had Uzis. I've just remembered that. I don't know how they obtained it. I think it's an Israeli rifle. But the Heckler -- before the war started, the police started using this in special units. It's shorter than the standard automatic rifle, the M-70, for example, which was a standard weapon. I think that this weapon was imported, and they started importing it before the war. They started importing it from the West.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, what calibre bullets a Heckler rifle would fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9-millimetre bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what calibre bullets an Uzi would fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also just mentioned that the paramilitary forces also had heavy weapons. Do you know what type of heavy weapons the paramilitary forces were equipped with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had various types of weapons, usually guns of a smaller calibre, 20-millimetre guns, then Pragas. These are mobile vehicles that have 30-millimetre guns mounted on them. They then had mortars. Some of them also had Pragas. I've already mentioned the Pragas, but they had multiple rocket launchers. They also had some special -- specially-modified weapons, so to speak. Some of them perhaps had even heavier weapons. But these are the weapons that they most frequently had. I was also told that they had a tank, but this wasn't in the Kosevo Brigade zone. There was no paramilitary unit of that kind that disposed -- that had tanks in that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know how these paramilitary forces received their ammunition for these various weapon systems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That surprised me too. And even today certain things aren't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than ammunition, do you know how these paramilitary forces received any other type of logistical support or supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very strange. Sometimes they even had more weapons than the legal army. So sometimes they would provide the army and the police with ammunition -- with these things. How they obtained it, I don't know. I don't know what their source was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You're aware, then, of instances, Witness, in which the paramilitary forces would actually be supplying the army with ammunition? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know, for example, that some of them had weapons and they would quite simply withdraw and leave those weapons and official army or police force would take possession of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, Witness, you mentioned, while being shown a document, weekend warriors. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. An order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if I understood what you said correctly, you told us that we could warriors were individuals who had, for example, leave approved for a couple of days and then did not return to their unit when that leave was over, and you characterised these people as weekend warriors. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I put to you that a weekend warrior was not someone who overstayed their leave but, rather, was someone who would come to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps zone of responsibility on weekends to engage in combat activities and during the week would return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that -- what you've said is similar, but I know what I said and what I am claiming. This occurred on several occasions. It wasn't just in the order that you saw. Requests were made to terminate weekend warring, warfare. So that had to do with people who decided themselves how they would come and go. They didn't adhere to the timetables or the plan that had been established by the command. That was one of the problems that was mentioned on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So there were, in fact, individuals who would come from outside the Sarajevo theatre and engage in combat activities on weekends and then return to their homes or areas outside of Sarajevo during the Monday through Friday work week. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that falls within the context of this order, and there weren't many such cases. And in my unit, this was not the case, because the people lived there. But if there were people who lived 10 or 20 kilometres in the interior, then he would go for a few days and then have a rest and then come again. Weekend warriors are warriors who have no discipline. That would be the right way to put it, because as the war continued, there were more and more weekend warriors. I don't know what the date of that order is, but it can't have been 1992. It could have been 1993 or 1994. Because later on people became tired and they made efforts not to go to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that we go into closed session for a few questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into -- private session will do, Mr. Mundis? It's just about spoken words?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Private session is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with the area of Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The brigade that you were assigned to was on the opposite side of the front lines from Kobilja Glava; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right flank -- yes, the right flank of the Kosevo Brigade had in front of it Kobilja Glava, yes, over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did forces of the Kosevo Brigade ever engage targets in Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Kobilja Glava, yes, in case of attacks. If they -- if fire was opened on them from that direction, they would act. And the fiercest attacks came from that direction, from the direction of Betanija, I mean, on Kosevo Brigade. The Kosevo Brigade sustained the fiercest attacks from that direction, from the direction of Betanija, and that was when we suffered -- when the brigades suffered the largest number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 3750A.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the Defence see it -- oh. Will the document be on the ELMO? I didn't know how we shall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the document is going to be put on the ELMO, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll all see what's the document about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if that could be zoomed out slightly, please. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the photographs that are depicted on the screen in front of you, P3750A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. This is a religious structure, a mosque. Now that you've told me that it was Kobilja Glava, then I assume it is the mosque at Kobilja Glava. But from the photograph itself, I wouldn't have been able to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I put to you that the photograph that you're looking at is in fact the mosque in Kobilja Glava, that that mosque was targeted throughout the war, and that the minaret was brought down towards the end of 1992. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps even earlier than that. But yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on, I'd like to know: When did the Prosecution show this document to the Defence? When was it disclosed to us? And we do not know if it was admitted, but the Defence would like to know when was this document disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When it is admitted, we'll hear from the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document has been admitted into evidence, so there should be no problem -- the black-and-white version. And this is a -- yes. The black-and-white version has been admitted into evidence, and then we asked for the colour version. But the objection has been withdrawn, so there's no -- please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so that I'm absolutely clear, Witness, the bottom photograph shows the destroyed mosque and the upper photograph shows the remains of the minaret. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite clear. Quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this is the -- this is the remains of the mosque in Kobilja Glava.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. If you say that it is, then it is. One could see it from the positions of the Kosevo Brigade, and that is what it looked like until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So from the positions of the Kosevo Brigade, you could clearly see this mosque throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could, yes, from some of the positions. From some points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The exhibit can be returned to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in early 1992, before the war broke out, the JNA surrounded the city of Sarajevo with heavy artillery. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area that I was in, that was not the case. That was not true. No such unit turned up there, and I do say that that is true, that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of JNA artillery units anywhere around the city of Sarajevo immediately prior to the war breaking out in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media reported that there were some army units on their move, that there were some such forces. But where exactly they were deployed, I do not know. I know that in the Kosevo Brigade's area, that is, in the area of the municipality of Centar, they were no such assignments before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I shall be happy to do that, with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you were asked to speak closer the microphone. I don't know whether it can be moved in your direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I shall do it immediately, Mr. President. But all this technology imposes on me, but let's see if I can do it the other way around. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I go back to what you said yesterday. Do you remember that yesterday the Prosecution asked you something about the pillage? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please elaborate on this. What was the reaction of the higher echelons of the army in your organisation with regard to the looting? What kind of measures were taken and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were, to all intents and purposes, impotent. We were powerless, at least as far as my brigade was concerned. There was no room for looting. I mean, in that area, there were no particular assets worth looting, but in Vogo -- there was this road from Ilidza-Rajlovac-Vogosca, towards Pale, Sokolac, and the eastern part of Sarajevo. And I mean in the beginning we took certain steps. We controlled this route, whilst we -- and I'm referring also to the civilian police at that time which operated in the brigade's area and which had its chief and its commander, and we tried to stop it then but it was impossible. The theft of Golfs is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I have to stop you, but my question did not concern the results but the measures that were taken, namely whether the military administration took any measures. Did it try to enforce them in order to stop the plunder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said it. Insofar as my brigade was concerned, it just so happened that its hands were the cleanest, because in its area of responsibility there was nothing to steal. However, through the area of responsibility passed quite a number of such people who had misappropriated certain things, and the civilian police was responsible for it and there were checkpoints. However, they were not strong enough and they couldn't really do anything worth mentioning, especially since the major part of their forces had also to be on the front line with the army units. I hope I've been precise enough on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to another of your answers, namely to what you said on page 53, line 20. And I'm referring to yesterday's record. You said on page 6117 at line 5 the question that you were asked was about sniping. At a certain point you said that to your mind those were not sniping cases technically speaking. And I will quote you in English. [In English] "It was the result of normal fire. It was the result of normal fire." [Interpretation] It was the result of normal fire. That is, just regular fire that was opened. What did you mean by this? That is, could you tell us what would you define as "normal," as "regular fire"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, from standard weapons without optical sights. That is -- that was a term that was adopted by both our and the other side. When a man -- when a soldier is killed by a single bullet, then you're automatically going to say it was a sniper. However, if it is at a distance of 200 metres, then automatic rifle or any other rifle can do that. So that in our brigade it says there are more than ten soldiers who were killed by snipers, but that was just the kind of lingo that we used. Actually, nobody can say whether it was an automatic rifle, a semi-automatic rifle, carbine, or whatever throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will interrupt you now. I have to interrupt you. Do you know -- I will rephrase my question. Did you in your military career in Sarajevo, did you come across the problem of stray bullets? Do you have any experience with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the term. And there were such cases too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And this problem of stray bullets, is it something which under fighting conditions happens frequently or seldom, or what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not a common occurrence. A stray bullet is a rare occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps may I ask you, what is a stray bullet, Mr. DP34? What is a stray bullet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not receive interpretation in English at this very moment. So could you please start again with your answer. I asked you what a stray bullet is, and we didn't receive translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll give you one example. It can happen during combat or it may be a day without any fighting. And my example is a quiet day. Now, somebody is hit perhaps 1 kilometre deep in the territory, and according to the knowledge that we have - and I'm referring to our side - a bullet could not have come normally from the adversary's side, that is, he could not be targeted because he simply could not see him, and then we say, "It was a stray bullet." That was a bullet fired which just happened to hit a man, like lottery, you know. Or it can be in combat. When it overshoots and the bullet flies over the target and hits somebody there, somebody who has not been seen by the man who fired that bullet. Do you understand my now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. So a stray bullet is a bullet that missed the target the shooter had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that too. Yes, that is possible too. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that from the circumstances you deduce whether a bullet was a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just remembered an instance when a man -- when a civilian was killed, and that was in the area of Debelja. And if you look at it, it's towards Mrkovici. Remember, that map that we saw, so it is at the very end of my left flank of our area of responsibility. And we noted that it was a stray bullet. Yes, the man was a civilian. I remember it well because I went to the spot and that was what the investigation showed. Now, of course how good is investigation in wartime, I don't know. But this was done by the civilian police because they were more qualified then we were to do that. So the conclusion was a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How could you exclude that this person was targeted, let's say, from a distance of four, five hundred metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean I didn't exclude that possibility. That possibility does exist, but it is not really very probable. If you could see the lay of the land there, then you would realise that it is impossible to see somebody there. From the distance of 500 metres, one couldn't see the whole figure. Perhaps the head only. But even with the best optical sights, you cannot see the head. So had he just been slightly lower -- because there was a hill and he was shielded. And the surface of the target was so small -- the area of the target was so small that you really need a very special eye, very special sights to be able to see that. So in that particular case, that was the conclusion. That was the kind of conclusion that was made, and I believe that it was, as likely as not, a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And along the same vein, how many, generally speaking -- how important is it to investigate the ground, the relief to be able to establish from one case to the other whether one was dealing with an accident, whether one was dealing with stray bullets, or was it more likely that it was something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that can play a role too. That is, the configuration, the relief, the lay of the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that it does not happen often. But apart from the stray bullet, when you spoke about that you told us about quiet days, about days which -- on which there was little fire. And on such days would you, for instance, use such days to reposition yourself, and would you notice then more such cases of the stray bullets? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I said: A stray bullet happens very seldom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The Prosecution would assert that this has gone way beyond the scope of the cross-examination with respect to sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you would please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I mean with your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yesterday you were also asked a number of questions - and I'm referring to page 62 - about what is termed a "standing order." You were asked this question with reference to the problems concerning systemic -- systematic defence. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you also said yesterday that there were certain places and in the trenches, against the certain walls of military facilities, that you also had certain rules about the humanitarian aid, that is, the Geneva Conventions, and that you had done that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not of the walls but at the entrance, yes. At the entrance into the trench, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Very good. So it was -- so it was there. And why at the entrance? Why at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that is where you can see it best, so that when soldiers get in, they can see it. It wasn't me. It was the commander who put it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And why was this reminder of the obligations about the human rights, why was it put up on there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again, beyond the scope of cross-examination. These questions -- this series of questions comes directly from the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please remove his headset in view of the time. I'd rather if he would remove the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first ask you, Mr. -- May I first ask you: Do you read or understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very, very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Usher, could you switch the screen of the witness to not the transcript. And could you please take your headphones off, Mr. DP34. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps if the same question could be asked with respect to French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you speak or understand any French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand any French at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then would you please take your headphones off. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. The question arises from the cross-examination in that the purpose of the questions asked by the Prosecution was to find out what kind of permanent order had been given to units and within what kind of context. We know that one of the positions that the Prosecution has adopted is that in military terms, the SRK did nothing in order to inform of the provisions that are used when there are armed conflicts or anything -- they didn't do anything to do for these provisions to be respected either. What I want to know is when one puts up a poster in very visible places, when one puts up the most essential elements that have to do with armed conflicts, shouldn't this be interpreted by everyone as a standing order, a permanent order stating that certain things should not be done? And if this is the case, in our opinion this is an order which doesn't have to be repeated on a daily basis to the officers, since it has been put up in a visible spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the purpose of the questions of the Prosecution rather than to the questions. [Interpretation] Which question were you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's exact. That's quite right, Mr. President. But there was an entire line of questions, page 55, line 1. I could find that. And it -- these questions had to do with the number or type of standing orders. And what we are saying is if one order is put up, this, too, should be considered as a standing order, And I wanted the witness to confirm this. And by the way, the intention seems quite obvious to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please put his headphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the question could be rephrased. I think there were four or five questions in one. So could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase it, Mr. President. I'll try and find the place where we stopped a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. My question is as follows: You explained to us about the fact these two pages were put up at the entrance or exit from the trenches. My question is: What was the purpose -- apart from the fact that one should see it as clearly as possible, what was the purpose, the main reason for which these two photocopies had been put up at the entrance or at the exit of these military installations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, so that the members of the army should be aware of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you also consider this to be a sort of standing order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would now like to move on to another subject. At page 60 yesterday you mentioned situations in which you -- the commanders spoke about problems of authority and you mentioned certain -- a certain commander who didn't want to respect a certain order or who hadn't fully complied with a certain order. Do you remember this situation? I'll rephrase that question, Witness. Yesterday the Prosecution asked you whether you were ever present at meetings where the problem of non-compliance with orders was discussed or the problem of not having executed orders. You said that you would discuss certain commanders who didn't carry out orders or who failed to fully carry out orders. Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, but I took the question to mean whether there were such cases when certain orders were not respected. That's how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, exactly. But my question is as follows: At these meetings that you attended and which were attended by brigade commanders or other high-ranking members of the military, can one imagine that at that level one might discuss the failure to respect orders or the violation of orders if this took place at the lowest level of the hierarchy, that is to say, if such failure to carry out orders or to fully carry out orders could be attributed to the troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I object. It was a leading question, but it's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. That's right, Mr. President. I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- about facts and not whether he could imagine -- everyone could imagine whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, within this context - and I mean at the level of meetings that took place with the chiefs of the brigades and in general at Lukavica - did you ever attend a meeting where one may have discussed the violation of orders at the level of the troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. It's a leading question. It's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- Mr. DP34 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase that, gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us -- you've told us that during these meetings you discussed sometimes that orders were not fully complied with, that is, not -- that they were disobeyed but they were not fully complied with. Could you tell us perhaps by giving examples whether this would -- something that happened on all levels or on certain levels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they discussed matters at a certain level, the level of the command of the brigade corps, or perhaps an independent regiment or battalion. That's the level at which discussions were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on any lower level -- not compliance on lower levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean company commanders, platoon, detachment commanders, a much lower level? No, I wasn't present at such meetings when such levels were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday, page 70, line 10, you declared that you never knew of and never received orders about targeting civilian features. Do you remember making this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that very clearly. And I would like to repeat that I never received any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'll now ask you a question which is purely hypothetical. Let's imagine - and it's a hypothesis - that you did receive an order from some military authority which you may have interpreted and understood as not being a legitimate order. Would you personally have executed such an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This kind of hypothesis how -- what would have happened if... Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is not greatly assisting the Chamber in determining what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: At page 7929 you spoke about the general agreement to exclude arms, heavy weapons -- to exclude heavy weapons around Sarajevo. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question then has to do with General Galic's participation in this agreement. Do you know whether General Galic participated actively in this agreement? Do you know whether he wanted this agreement to be implemented? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As corps commander I can tell you that he issued orders according to which that should be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know when these orders were issued with regard to the conclusion of the agreement -- the establishment of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. You know that there were several such agreements, and on each occasion after the agreement an order was issued from the main staff to the corps, from the corps to the brigades, and these weapons were then withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as your brigade is concerned and your duties, to what extent was this agreement implemented?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 per cent. UNPROFOR was present. I've already mentioned that. It was a small unit. It was easy to control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I know. I know. Thank you. I want to go back to the question of paramilitary troops. Page 83 you said -- but before I ask you this question, I'll ask you something else. Can you say -- can you tell us since which date UNPROFOR was at your positions? Do you know? Do you remember the month, the period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but I know it was summer 1992. That's when the first observers arrived. I remember that very clearly. I think there was a Polish man, a Portuguese man, and there was a translator too. It was early in the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Tell me, did these men remain there throughout the period? How long did they remain there, these observers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the observers -- the UN observers were there continuously. Not the ones I've mentioned, but observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And that includes the dates the 23rd and the 24th of December, 1992 up until the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again, this is beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution asked an entire series of questions that had to do with heavy weapons and the exclusion zone, and I think that the witness is free to respond if one wants to know whether -- whether this exclusion zone was respected and also whether there were UNPROFOR men who were there before this took place, before the withdrawal of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a question whether the witness is free to answer a question but whether you're free to put a question to the witness. The subject has been touched upon very briefly. You're similarly allowed to ask the question you just raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you briefly tell us about this. These military officials, were they present during the period mentioned, 24th of December, 1992, 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained to me -- before doing so, could you please take your headphones off for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber has reconsidered. We'll allow the witness to answer the question, but if this would be an introductory question to other events which on the basis of the dates might be true, that's not a matter that has been raised in cross-examination. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you answer the question. Witness, could you answer the question as briefly as possible; that is to say, the question that has to do with the presence of the military observers at the period mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise as to the day, but during that period they were present. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I please just try to -- You're talking about military observers. Are you referring to UNMOs or are you referring to UNPROFOR troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm referring to both of them. They were mixed up, the UN and UNPROFOR observers. The UNPROFOR observers were already there in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we sometimes make a distinction between what we call UNMOs, military observers, and UNPROFOR troops, which is not exactly the same. Do you say it's the same or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be precise. We consider them to be the same, but I know it's not the same. But for the army they were the UN forces. That's how they were viewed, as the United Nations. So they were considered to be the same but in fact they weren't the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you answered the question in the affirmative, did you refer to anything else than military observers in observation posts within the zone of responsibility of your brigade, or did you refer to anything else than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was thinking of military observers but also UN observers. To be quite frank, I didn't distinguish between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about the problem of paramilitary groups. That was page 83. And you also said that there were certain arrests. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On whose initiative, on whose orders were these repressive and punitive measures taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, on the orders of the brigade commander, and then of the battalion commander. In the first case, I was the one who issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether in relation to this desire to intervene and to punish there were any orders at a superior level or at superior levels? And I'm still referring to the problem of paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll rephrase that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any other orders that concerned this problem, the issue of intervening in the case of paramilitary troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in other units?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I'm not thinking about other units. Perhaps other orders in the structure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, I said that that was a problem that was discussed at regular meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Which ordinary -- which regular meetings are you referring to? At what level were they held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, I would like to place page 3 of document 1853 on the ELMO. It's a document that was provided yesterday. And I'd like to draw the witness's attention to the fact that I would like him to read out item F. It only consists of six words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Accelerate and encourage the work of military courts."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, in response to a question put to you by the Prosecution about punitive measures taken by a brigade, you said that there weren't any court-martials that had been established. Having read this item, which says "accelerate and stir up the work of military courts," what can you tell us about this matter, that is to say, about the army's intention to encourage these phrasings that have to do with establishing military courts? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this court was never established in the unit that was under any command I don't know what the date of this document is. When the state of war was declared in part of the territory, then military courts were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I would now like to move on to the question of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP34, just a clarification. You said "when the state of war was declared, then military courts were established." When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in 1995 for a brief period of time. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it was established in the 3rd Sarajevo, but there weren't any cases to be heard at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that there were never taken any decisions. Is that correct? Yes. If there's need to confer, could it please be done in such a way that it's beyond the -- what the witness can hear. Yes. So 1995 the state of war was declared. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, your answer is applicable to your brigade, but what do you know, since you said that this court wasn't established in your unit, what do you know about what happened to such courts in other units, in other brigades? Do you know anything about this; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the level of the brigades but at higher levels there was a court in existence, but I didn't have any contact with it. I said how those -- I told you how those two murders were dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But the court in question - and I'm talking about the level of the corps - was this a court-martial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the corps, there was an entire judiciary system, and that's why it could also be a military court. But I didn't have any contact with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, merely to remind the Chamber of -- that this exhibit was of the 12th of September, 1992, so as not to mix it up with other timings in question that were asked of the witness. I believe that now the time is perfect for a break, Mr. President, unless you have some other ideas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- If you would just grant me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.04 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for providing the translation, Ms. Pilipovic. The Chamber has been informed that in the presence of the witness discussions took place, that could be overheard by the witness, between you, General Galic, and Defence counsel. This causes -- because I have drawn your attention to the fact that this is not permissible. Therefore, we'll change the order. First have the witness to leave, and of course that's a total waste of time. If the Defence would refrain from doing that, the Chamber would not have been in a position to order that the witness first should leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Enough has been said about it. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. The apologies are accepted but do not take away the necessity of this measure, which the Chamber regrets that it has to take. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of what the Chamber has just decided and with respect to earlier warnings to the same effect, the Prosecution would respectfully request that the re-examination not be allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you were informed, you would have certainly been told that when I saw -- that when I heard that General Galic needed to say whatever, I -- you should have seen that I immediately approached him to say, "Let us not discuss it in the courtroom." But it happens less and less often, but at times there are noises which can be heard but it happens less and less often. And contrary to what happens in the courtroom -- we are usually in the Courtroom number III, that is -- the distance between the accused and his counsel is much bigger, and therefore, he speaks out more -- he speaks out louder. I have, that is true, two pairs of headsets, but I do not have two pairs of ears. Therefore, he needs to speak louder. If now the re-examination is prohibited for this reason, so let it be done. But the Defence, of course, will object to this infringement of its rights. But accusations which are based on this, if we are forbidden to do that, will they do it or shall we -- should we not do it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the Defence to continue its re-examination and at the same time draws the attention both of Defence counsel but also your attention, General Galic, that it is in your own interest to avoid such situations, since the type of response, as the Prosecution has requested -- "response," I mean the kinds of consequences to be attached to what happened are not unimaginable. So therefore, it's in your own interest, and certainly a way can be found to start communication without speaking loud. I'm certain that the security officer will certainly draw the attention of Defence counsel to the fact that you, General Galic, might want to speak to Defence counsel. And as you noticed, I always and this Chamber has always given full opportunity to confer if necessary. But you're taking risks if you do it the way it has been done. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Could you tell us how much time you'd still need approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen minutes, less time. I want to say that I was not perfectly interpreted in page 35, line 13 to 15 what I was asking the Prosecutor, in view of my intervention, but I -- I see that there is absolutely no response to that. However, I will now resume my examination, and thank you for your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Will you please concentrate now on a different aspect of the question that interests us, and that is the photographs of a destroyed mosque that you just saw which were shown to us. You responded to a question that it is -- it was possible that this mosque was destroyed prior to the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said. That is what I said. That is exactly what I said in French, that the witness said that it was possible that the mosque had been destroyed before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a good reflection. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So I'm resuming. In replying to the question by the Prosecution, you said that that was quite possible and that it was quite possible that this happened before the expiration of 1992. However, you did not give us the date or the period. So my question is as follows: Which period do you have in mind -- which period did you have in mind when you said that it was quite possible that this destruction happened before the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, let me say that the mosque was not destroyed by the Kosevo Brigade - that is number one - and the local population is aware of that at Kobilja Glava. Number two, I said that as far as my memory serves me that it was still warm. So I think it must have been either early autumn or summer when that happened. I cannot give you the precise date. One can see it better from the positions of another brigade, but it was destroyed -- I think it was either summer or early autumn 1992, and it remained in that state until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned "summer," can you be more precise? Could you please give us a month or perhaps use something to trigger your memory. I don't know whether -- was it the harvest time or -- I don't know. If you can't do that, then it's a pity, but ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I can't. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17971 to 17979.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like us now to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all. Not at all. I'll rephrase my question -- I'll repeat my question: Do you remember the date more or less when you took the decision to lay these anti-personnel mines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were laid throughout the war period in continuity, because a minefield can be disturbed. A dog or a wild animal can enter a minefield and can activate a mine. And with the passage of time and because of the weather, it's possible for mines to become defective. As we say, they can rust. And in the course of combat activities, certain mines activated. And then the minefields have to be repaired. There are plans. The engineers have the plans of minefields, and they use these plans -- the engineers use these plans to renovate, to update the minefield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answer. I don't know if you remember the order dated the 12th of September [Realtime transcript read in error "December"], 1992 in which there are various items and you read out paragraph 1. Perhaps, Madam Registrar, you could assist us. It is document 1453, I think. With regard to this document, I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 1. You are following me. And I'm going to quote from this paragraph in English: [In English] "Prepare the most persistent and decisive defence on reached lines." [Interpretation] Then a few lines further on it says: [In English] "With liberation and reaching the important part of the town, structures in its vicinity and settlements," so on so, end of quote. [Interpretation] What you understand from this order are two different things: First of all, to ensure that defence is mounted, and then to advance in order to liberate parts of the town. Is this a strategic plan that was implemented through tactical plans? Were you yourself charged with carrying out an attack and with liberating parts of the town, and which parts, if this was the case? Could you perhaps explain the reasoning behind this order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This item in this order is totally clear to me. Here they're saying that all units should ensure a most persistent and decisive defence on the lines that were reached. As I have already said, that was the main order that my unit had throughout the war. And then it also says that certain units should attempt to move in Donji Kotorac, Hrasnica, Butmir, Kolonija. This was the -- on the other side, from the northern theatre. That's southern side, or rather, the south-east. That's how I understand it. It's very clear. So they're not giving the entire corps the task of attacking, if I have understood you correctly. It says, "The unit or the units that are on the Kotorac, Hrasnica, Butmir, Sokolovic, Kolonija axis. I think I'm being quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So with reference to this sentence, "parts of the town," do you know which part it concerns and which troops were responsible for carrying out this attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says which parts of the town are concerned. And the units that were in that zone of responsibility had this task. As far as I can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I apologise for interrupting you, but after having said "Mojmilo, Stupska," these are examples. There are others. How do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mojmilo, Stupska Petlja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the dots, how do you understand that. That means, "et cetera", doesn't it? That doesn't mean -- at least not in the English version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be understood this way too. But Mojmilo, Stupska Petlja, and what is in the brackets. And then it says, "And settlements." But these are features. When you say "features," they are referring to important features, perhaps to Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But all I want to know: Am I to take it that you weren't familiar with detailed plans, tactical plans for the implementation of this strategic plan, if I may call it that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an operative plan, in my opinion. And I wasn't familiar with the details, nor were any -- nor were any of the commanders from the northern or north-western battlefield familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this an issue that was raised at your meetings within the framework of the corps command? I mean the implementation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've understood the question. Yes, this was an issue that was raised too, but more as a matter of principle. But this concerned the brigade commanders on these axes -- or rather, these units. I don't know how this had been imagined, but these commanders compiled specific orders for certain cases. But I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the plan, Lukavica 93 - I apologise if I haven't pronounced it correctly - does this mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this also part of the implementation of this order? What were the objectives of the Lukavica 93 plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spent a longer period of time there, and it was more focussed on the outer ring there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are just two matters I would like to clarify. The first one has to do with the use of mortars. I think that you said that you couldn't be sure or certain that the shelling of the hospital near your lines was the result of a firing error. Do you remember in the course of your testimony you said that a hospital had been targeted. I'm talking about a hospital on your side. It was about a kilometre from your lines, and it had been hit by mortar shells, and you did not exclude the possibility of there being a margin of error. That is your testimony, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that hospital was less than 2 kilometres from the lines. I think that that is what I said. I think I said 1 kilometre from the lines, but that's not important. And secondly, we didn't expand on this question yesterday. There was a lot of discussion. We analysed why this was done, and there are several possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in answer to a question put to you by the Defence, the Defence suggested that perhaps this shelling was the result of an error, a firing error. And you did not exclude this possibility, if I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly - I don't know whether I've finished with this - the direction from which the shell came was determined with certainty. But whether the person who fired that shell from the Federation army, whether he was targeting the hospital, this is something that no one can know. But it is considered that he fired because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But as a member of the military, a professional member of the military, do you accept that a margin of error of 1.000 metres is a possibility, a margin of error of 1 kilometre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not of 1 kilometre. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But for you the margin of error could be between -- could amount to what kind of distance? How many metres, more or less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on a number of factors. But it could be 100 or 200 metres. If it misses a target, an elevation, perhaps, or some high feature, if it misses it, then it doesn't fall vertically. It will continue its trajectory and will fall a little further on but not -- it won't fly -- cover an additional distance of a kilometre, at least when a mortar shell is concerned. But artillery shells can go further. They can advance further. But if the margin of error is to the left or to the right, the margin of error is not so great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But I'm talk about mortars. And you say, if I've understood you correctly, that a margin of error of 100 metres or 200 metres is quite plausible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- you're referring to the specific case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I'm speaking in general. For you, as a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible in certain conditions, but not even such an error should be made. A good marksman can be very precise. So then it might be a matter of metres. But all I said was that such a margin of error is also possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you as a member of the military, if you use a mortar and given the margin of error that is possible, would this restrict the usage of mortars if the targets are in the vicinity of protected features, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. My very last question has to do with paramilitary groups. As far as you know, were they structured, organised, or were they dispersed groups that didn't form an organisational unit, a unit within a hierarchy of one way or another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I said that there were a number of such groups. And it's very difficult to talk about how they were organised. Even today this isn't clear for me. For me some of them were classical Mafia groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they acted independently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Have I understood you correctly? Do you mean were they -- were they linked up? Were these groups linked to each other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, those groups. Were they linked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, paramilitary group 1 and paramilitary group 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's possible that they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how did you arrive at this conclusion -- how do you think they were supplied? You said they had weapons which were similar to the ones you had. They had the means of communication. If these groups were dispersed -- you were in the field, so could you tell us in more detail how they functioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, to be precise, I think that the right way of putting it would be to say that their weapons were better than the ones that the regular army and the regular police force had. The arms they had were lighter. They were more modern. They didn't have standard weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you also mentioned a tank, perhaps, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that one of those units -- one of those formations also had a tank at the beginning of the war. Later on -- I don't know what happened, but that wasn't in the zone of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you personally are not aware of how they were supplied. You don't know where they obtained their weapons and these means of combat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can guess, but the heavier weapons could only have been obtained through corrupt channels. Someone who had those weapons perhaps exchanged the weapons for a personal vehicle. You understand? Because at the beginning of the war, it was chaos. The situation was confused and the commanders who were from the army, some of them left, left the unit, left their weapons. This is an assumption, because I don't know how else these weapons would have been obtained. If they had been obtained through legal channels, they would have been placed under the command. No one will give a tank to someone and just let him drive away. It should be placed under the command of the unit that provided the tank. You understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But my very last question: In the end, was the corps able to place these paramilitary groups under its command, make them part of their structure, or did they remain independent, in inverted commas, and did they act as they saw fit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- or rather, I'm claiming that the corps command and the brigade command in whose zone such units were located and higher commands than the corps commands and the state organs, the legal state organs, they were always attempting to solve this matter. But it was very difficult to do for the simple reason that you had to have special forces to solve this problem. There would have been a conflict within the zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I to understand that what you are saying is that in the zone of responsibility of the Romanija Corps these groups always existed and the corps was not able to assimilate them, to place them under their command? They existed -- they were there until the summer of 1994. Do you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've understood you, Your Honour. But this is an example which the prosecutor provided with regard to one of the paramilitary groups when he put a question to me. For example I thought that group had been placed under his command, according to the information I've been provided with. But I understand the Prosecution does not agree with this. So if the group remained as a group and placed itself under the command of the corps, the brigade, or some battalion, or the main staff, in my opinion, that no longer traditional paramilitary formation. But if it acts and is under no one's command, then it's a paramilitary formation. They are acting independently. You don't know under whose command they are. One doesn't know how they obtained weapons, food, ammunition. One doesn't know what their tasks are or what the reason for the existence of such groups is. In such a case this group is a real paramilitary group. Their task is to spread confusion, to loot, to act in a corrupt manner, et cetera, et cetera. I don't know if I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Page 44, line 12, it should read "September 12th, 1992," not "December."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I also -- that's my recollection that I understood September. Mr. DP34, I've got a few questions for you as well. I would like to seek some clarifications. You told us that the cemetery -- the Kosevo cemetery was not used any more, and you referred to a cemetery in Bare that instead would be used. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did the Kosevo cemetery stop to function? From when on was it not used any more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the cemetery -- there was the Kosevo cemetery and there were three cemeteries that I mentioned. They stopped using it, well, perhaps 10 or 15 years before the war, at least, or maybe 20 years before the war. And then the big Bare cemetery was opened. The cemetery remained, but it wasn't active. In fact, all three cemeteries were closed because they made a central cemetery called Bare, and that's where the funerals were organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was Bare more to the east from Kosevo or more to the west, north, or south?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kosevo, it's to the north-west. It's north-west of Kosevo. It's from the -- it's on the road that leads from Sarajevo to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could perhaps the map 1834, I think it is, Defence exhibit, be shown to the witness. Could you indicate whether the Bare hospital appears on this map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can be seen quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand your answer well -- if perhaps you could point at it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. It says "61," and then "Bare" above the figure. It's a big complex. It's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the number "61," and above the number 61 it says "Bare."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At what distance would that be approximately from the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Kosevo hospital? Just a minute. Well, perhaps a kilometre and a half. A kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that cemeteries were of no -- were of no military interest to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't. And in the Bare cemetery, perhaps a soldier or two could be registered, not more than that. But it was held by the Federation army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I -- you said that the Kosevo cemetery was not used any more since the -- already from a moment prior to the war. Was it not being used during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we had, it was. As far as I know, the Catholic and Orthodox cemetery and the Lav cemetery, that is, the atheist or Partisan cemetery, as it was called, they were all used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So during the war the cemeteries were used, not only the Bare cemetery.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bare cemetery was not used during the war; I am sure of that. I -- as far as I know, there were no burials there, but people were buried in those other cemeteries and elsewhere too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
