utterances.text: Then my next question would be the following: You told us that during the meetings your attention was drawn to the prohibition of firing at civilians because the damage to your image in the eyes of the International Community would be caused by that. What was your image in the eyes of the International Community in respect of firing at civilians? Whether right or wrong. I'm not talking about whether it was right or wrong, but what was the image, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must check if I understood your question. I understand that you asked me what reputation did I enjoy with the International Community. That is how I got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not you yourself. But when it was discussed that the opening of firing at civilians would be prosecuted because such behaviour would cause a lot of damage to your image in the eyes of the International Community- not your personal image, but I take it you referred to the image of your armed forces- could you tell us what, according to your knowledge, the image of your armed forces was in the eyes of the International Community.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a higher level, not accessible to me. I know there were problems from the media. I know that both politically and militarily there were problems of this kind. I know that. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Problems of what kind? You said "problems of this kind."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the image, the reputation. That is what you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be perhaps even more clear. According to your knowledge, was the image- I'm not saying right or wrong- was the image that your forces would shoot at civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a reservation here. The most competent answer to this could be given by the observers and UNPROFOR men who were there. And when talking with them in the area where I was, my impression was that there were not any major problems. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- You told us that because of the image in the International Community, you got certain instructions, instructions in respect of shooting at civilians. What, according to your knowledge, whether it was your brigade or anything else, whether true or not true -- what were you told or what did you know was the image of your armed forces in the eyes of the International Community that needed attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is how I put it, and I will repeat it: We were being cautioned not to open fire, not only against civilians but civilian facilities as well, not to open indiscriminate fire because it contributed to a bad image with the International Community, which is quite natural, and I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you tell us what in your perception or in the perception of those with whom you discussed this this image was. Let me put the question a different way to you: Shooting at civilians, firing at civilians, if you want to prevent that to happen, you could just give an order to say "Don't fire at civilians." But you added in your answer that special attention was drawn to the fact that this would cause a lot of damage to your image in the eyes of the International Community. So what I'm trying to find out is what your perception- you and those with whom you discussed this- what your perception was about your image in the eyes of the International Community.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it varied from one stage to the other and from one period to the other. For a while we thought that we enjoyed a good image and that the army as such- that is what we are talking about- and then later on it came into question. This question goes beyond my level, my rank -- my ranking in the armed forces. I think you would agree with me. I mean, these are things that should be assessed by people at a level higher even than a corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said the image changed from good to more problematic. In what respect? Were you considered to be a coward army or a -- what changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, you are really asking me questions which are well beyond my competence. I really do not know how to do it. Perhaps I said something a while ago but a little different and then you understood me wrong. It does not mean that the fame we enjoyed was first good then bad. I think it sort of went up and down, up and down. That is -- there were so many political negotiations and military negotiations at high levels, of course I had no access to them. When commanders of the main staffs met, corps commands met, and I am simply telling you that that was well beyond my horizontal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say "ups and downs," what would be up and what would be down? I'm just trying to find out what you considered to worsen your image, your reputation, and what would be a better reputation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could draw conclusions mostly through the media. That was the chief source. We followed the media. So at times one gained the impression that an agreement would be reached at the highest level and that peace would come finally, and then it falls through and it starts all over again, and it confused foot soldiers and lower-ranking officers. What role could I play in those spheres which were loftier political spheres. All I could do in my area was comply with the customs of war or, rather, Geneva Conventions. And that was the end of it. All the rest belonged in the higher political spheres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say that you learned these things from the media, what media did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accessible media. Well, television and radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What television could you receive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received -- well, to begin with, none when there was no electricity. But then we could watch the television of the Republika Srpska and television of the Federation, and we watched them both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what would they say? You say you learned about it from the media. What would they say, since -- you're talking about your reputation. In what way did you find out that your reputation became worse or better?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can conclude that from the unfolding of the events. There was a propaganda war, if I may call it that. If you watched the news of the Federation and the news in Republika Srpska, you would get two different sets of news or, rather, two different commentaries or perceptions of the situation. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would shooting at civilians be a part of that media war as well, your armed forces being blamed for shooting at civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that happened. We heard such news. And on the other hand, our news said that that was not true and vice versa, and vice versa. We had a conventional media war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you have spoken about your image in the eyes of the International Community, did you fear that such reports on firing at civilians would harm your image?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I was fearing it. I was more than aware of it. Of course destruction of civilian targets or firing at civilians, of course, would sully our image with the International Community, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that also have been one of the reasons why you got the instructions certainly not to fire at civilians, because this would damage your image?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I definitely think that that was one of the reasons; perhaps the main reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you explained during these meetings that this was one of the issues involved, why you got instructions definitely not to fire at civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just said. It was said orally in the corps and repeatedly said that it would tarnish the image and reputation of the army and the society as such. That is, not only the military but the whole people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were -- would you know which of the media was telling the truth? You said you could see the Federation television. You could see the Republika Srpska television. How did you know beyond your zone of responsibility which of the media was telling the truth, if any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe you already answered with the end of your question. I don't think that either side spoke the truth. I really think that. Or rather, that they -- that there were exaggerations on both sides. And only somebody who was neutral could supply an objective -- could supply objective coverage. But that was not accessible to us. Perhaps some television station in Europe or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you discuss among each other how to contradict if not true any of these media reports, specifically on sniping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area,- and I have already said that,- there was no sniper activity either on our side or from the other side. There wasn't really. If there was any, it was negligible, far from what happened in other parts of the city, where the conditions were different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But did you ever discuss - I'm talking about the meetings - also when it was not about your zone of responsibility, how to deal with these allegations on both sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the sniping, there was very little discussion about it. And as a problem, at the corps level -- I mean, that problem was much less discussed than, for instance, what I have said already about the targeting of civilian objectives with artillery fire and such like. But there were objections and protests from our side that the other side was engaged in sniping in some areas, so Grbavica, Dobrinja, and - just a moment - Nedzarici, yes. Nedzarici. Those local commanders reported that that was how it happened there. And those were areas where it was possible, where it was possible to engage in that kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have another question for you: You told us today that you -- that the court in which the two persons suspected of murder were tried, that that could have been a military court. Since you had no contact with those courts, you said it could have been a military court. Do you remember that? If you would like me to read that part of your testimony, I'd be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I don't think that those were my words. But I said -- can say exactly. In the first case, it wasn't a military court. I think I said it two days ago -- when was it? When I started. It was in the very early days of the war, so that there was no such court. And the second case I think was also dealt with by a civilian court, but it was the military authorities which started a protest -- or started the procedure, or rather, the investigation was conducted by the military authorities, but I think that the court itself was a civilian court and they were in civilian prisons, both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to have a clarification of what you say today and what you said yesterday. You said they were tried in a civil court. And yesterday you explained that by saying in the area - and you referred both to the brigade and to the corps level - that when there was no state of war yet declared, that there were no military courts and there was no court-martial functioning. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you. I don't know whether the parties have any additional question, related to questions from the Bench. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone or come closer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm talking about September 1992 and the order. There was one important matter, and that was a question which was asked of you by Judge El Mahdi. Can you tell us, were places such as those mentioned in brackets such as Mojmilo appear as places which are important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me? Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I thought you were about to add something. Mojmilo was very important because it was a major fire point which faced the corps command. That is, it could -- it was a menace to the corps command and localities there, and that was why it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about the second one of these places, I mean, Stupska Petlja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stupska Petlja, I do not know what the commander meant when he issued that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now I'd like you -- and this is the same series of questions -- and I'd like to ask you about Butmir, which is also mentioned or Hrasnica, Sokolovic. What do you know? How important were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not -- I did not speak about features. It may be an interpretation problem. I am talking about places or localities. I said, and I repeat, that it is at the other end of the city, on the completely other side, and that I knew very little about that area. And anything that I said -- that would not go beyond assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Also following up on questions asked by His Honour Judge El Mahdi. You were asked about mines, their type, their laying, and so on and so forth. Now, the question is as follows: Would you define as a mine what we are talking about as an offensive or a defensive weapon? What would you say a mine is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is exclusively a defensive weapon, a conventional weapon. It is in all armies like that and we learn it at school. You cannot throw a mine and then advance. If you are to advance, you have to first remove the mines from a minefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I go back now to another question which Judge El Mahdi asked you, and that had to do with the hospital and firing errors. Your answer was that an error of 100 to 200 metres was technically possible. And my question is: Does your answer apply to all calibres, or does it hold true of only some calibres? Perhaps some other calibres can have a bigger error, some smaller, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have already said that. It varies with the weapon. For instance, a gun, if it misses, that projectile can overreach 10 kilometres. It depends on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we are talking about mortars, and we know that generally speaking there are three calibres, 62, 81 - 82, and 120. These are the three chief calibres that we are interested in. Now, what are the margins of error? Do they vary depending on the calibre of mortar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure it can vary. Although, I must say that I am not an artillery man. I am not a gunner, so -- but, yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke about paramilitaries. Now, my additional question arising from the questions asked by the Chamber: Do you know if the adversary forces also had paramilitary forces and analogous problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a new subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely agree. I couldn't agree more. I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And now I am talking about APCs, about armoured vehicle, about tanks. You spoke to us about a tank which operated freely and which belonged to a paramilitary unit. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. I did not see it with my own eye, but I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. My first question -- and you just told us you never saw it. My second question is as follows: This tank, as something of a free-lancer -- not part of the complete integrated military structure -- did this tank exist and operate when it was integrated and when General Galic took over the command? That is, as of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I may be incorrect, but I don't believe this arose from a question posed by one of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please indicate where it arises from one of our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it seems to me -- it seems to me that a question by Judge El Mahdi to this witness indicates -- no. No, it was like this: I believe that Judge El Mahdi said himself, and I believe that you spoke about a tank which was held by paramilitaries. I believe there was a question which was phrased more or less like that and the witness obviously followed up and gave his answer. I can check it, but I believe that that is how the question was asked and then answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... As far as I remember, the witness once mentioned the word "tank" at the very end of a an answer to a question of Judge El Mahdi, which was the following question: "But you personally were not aware of how they were supplied. You don't know where they obtained their weapons and these means of combat." So the question was about how -- and then part of the answer I'm referring to is that -- the last part of the answer is: "No one will give a tank to someone and just let him drive away. It should be placed under the command of the unit that provided the tank. You understand?" That was, as far as I can see, the only way this issue was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I don't think that there was a specific question as to tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll repeat what I said. I think I remember Judge El Mahdi saying the following, and I think that I heard you say that there was a tank in the hands of the paramilitary groups and a question was asked about this. I'll try and find the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it. If you could assist me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could assist, Mr. President, page 50, line 13 on my transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it now. It reads: "But you also mentioned a tank, perhaps if I understood you correctly." And that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the part that I was referring to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You can put a question -- we have now found the source. You can put a question in relation to that question and the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You answered the question that Judge El Mahdi put to you, you don't really know what happened because it was outside your zone of responsibility. Nevertheless, do you know whether this tank remained or was ever active there during the period that General Galic was in command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I can't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, look at the clock. Would it be possible to conclude in -- shortly, or otherwise we'll have a break. You took already quite some time in re-examination. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another four questions, I think, but that could be quite quick -- three questions. But we could have a break and continue later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Since there might be no further questions, we could expect you to finish in a couple of minutes. And I ask the cooperation of the interpreters and technicians to stand as long as the tape goes. So we are limited by the tape. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The other issue concerns the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, apart from the Serbian language, which other languages can you understand perfectly well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only understand the Serbian or, rather, Serbo-Croat perfectly well. This is the language I learned at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, am I to infer that you yourself had no access to French, German, or English press?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the war, the press -- our own press that was published in the territory of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. I'm talking about the foreign press. Did you have access to it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Throughout the wartime period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the causes of the negative image, the negative impression left by your army and presented in the international media, and you were asked certain questions about being afraid of this image with regard to the targeting of civilians. My question has to do with the following: What was the main reason in your opinion for not targeting civilians? What was the main reason for not firing on civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it was never necessary. It would be absurd. It has no military effect. It only has a quota effect but no military objective is attained like this. It only -- it can only cause the enemy side to take revenge. That's quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said "firstly." What about the second reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you -- what else did you ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said "firstly." I don't know if there is a secondly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, secondly, I never received any such orders, if I have understood your question correctly. There was no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to interrupt you. I would appreciate it if you could concentrate on the question. What was the main reason, the primary reason, if you know the answer, for not opening fire on civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP34 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the primary reason was humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. DP34, this concludes your testimony in this court. You've spent a lot of time here. You've answered a lot of questions, both of the parties and quite some questions of the Bench. I thank you for coming to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to thank you, and I wish you all the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The documents, I'd prefer to deal with them at a later stage since -- otherwise, we would have to pull the curtains up first, and we could do that in due course. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I just need to know what the last number will be for the document that I will be showing the witness for whom protective measures have been taken. I think it's number 1836. I'd just like to check that. Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number will be D1837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then first turn into closed session before we start examining the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, Mr. DP36 -- and that's how we will call you, because protective measures have been granted in respect of you. That means that we'll not use your own name and that your face cannot be seen by the outside world. Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text has been handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. DP36. Mr. Usher, the curtains may be pulled up again. Mr. DP36, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Defence. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DP36, good day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start asking you a series of questions, I will show you a document. And could you confirm whether the details are correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: The details are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP36.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask some questions about Mr. DP36 himself. So could we go into private session while the witness is answering these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even when you ask them. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, you said that you retired in the year 2000. We'll be talking about the 1992, 1993, 1994 period. My first question is: Where were you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: In 1992 I was in the military historical institute in Belgrade. In 1992 I was working in the military historical institute in Belgrade. I was working there as a researcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. DP36, tell us, according to you, when did the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina break out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: I followed the events very closely, and I went to Sarajevo for the weekend on several occasions because my family went to Sarajevo from Split -- or rather, to Ilidza. So even in 1991 I noticed that there were people walking around the town with military equipment. They were wearing berets, et cetera. And in 1992, as early as February and March, war seemed inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that in February and March war was inevitable, can you tell us whether you noticed this when you went to visit your family in Sarajevo -- did you notice this in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my wife and son were there. My daughter remained in Split because she married a Croat. Even at that time I encountered barricades somewhere around the beginning of March when I was returning to Belgrade from Ilidza I stopped at Sirokaca. And the police force -- I suppose they were the reserve police forces, the MUP, they tried to search me. I said I was a member of the military and that only the military police could search me, and I passed through without any problems then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, can you tell us when did the war in Sarajevo break out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: According to what I could see in the daily press and on the television, the war started at the beginning of April, the 4th, the 5th, and the 6th of April, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 from the month of April onwards, can you tell us where you lived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: A minute ago I said that I had -- I worked in the military historical institute in a building where the personnel department of the former JNA is located. Since there was the threat of war and serious incidents and conflicts had broken out, I reported to the personnel department and asked them to transfer me to another army in order to be close to my family. They wrote an order, and with that order on the 22nd of April I went to another army district, to the 2nd army district. I used a helicopter to get there. I arrived in Pale on the 22nd, late in the evening, and I went to the commission centre in the Turist Biro Hotel. That was the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, thank you. On the basis of what you have just told us, can I then interpret it as your decision to come and live in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: I didn't go to live in Sarajevo. I was a professional military man, but I wanted to do it regularly with the order and my re-posting to be as a disposal of the 2nd army district as long as it existed. And besides, I would also be in the area where I was born, because I don't think it would be particularly ethical if anything happened there to have my family there and me to be far away from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, can you tell us precisely, between 1992 - that is, we shall be talking as of April 1992, when you say you came to that area - until December 1994 -- until autumn 1994, that is, we're interested in the early days of August 1994, did you live in the territory of the city of Sarajevo? And when I say"live," I mean were you in service? And if yes, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Well, I came with that order to the 2nd army district. But because of the war and the interruption of communications, that is, asphalt roads were cut off, I could not get off in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, I'm sorry. Can you just tell us briefly what was the period of time that you lived there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Well, in Pale I was from the 22nd of April until the 30th of April, when I was ordered to report to the 2nd army district, and the only road I could take to Lukavica was very poor, via Tvrdimic. It was a forest path, a dirt track that would take you two hours to get there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: DP36, I apologise. And I will interrupt you once again because -- simply because I want you to tell us something that is relevant for the -- for future questions. If you were in area of Sarajevo, it was from what date until what date? Can you give us the details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: From the 22nd of April until the 22nd of June, 1992. That was when I was in the area of the Sarajevo district. On the 30th, I went down to Lukavica, was authorised by General --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP36, now when you told us that between the 22nd of April until the 22nd of June, 1992, am I to take it that it was only then when you were there? That is what -- I asked you about the period until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: On the 22nd of June, 1992 I went back to Belgrade, and then on the 1st of April, once again, I arrived in the territory of Sarajevo and I stayed there until August 1994. In other words, from the 1st of April, 1993 until August 1994, the 1st of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let us try to sum up. Mr. DP36, in the territory of the city of Sarajevo, you were from the 22nd of April until the 22nd of June, 1992, and then after that you returned, and from the 1st of April, 1993 until August 1994 you remained in that territory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, in view of the time that you spent there, I will ask you a few questions concerning the period when you were there between the 22nd of April until the 22nd of June. Did you at that time hold a certain duty in the 2nd army district? And if so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: I arrived in the command of the 2nd army district on the 1st of May, in the afternoon, and I went to the department for morale and information. That was the command at Bistrik. And I stayed there until the 3rd of May in the afternoon, again, when there was the attack on Dobrovoljacka Street, when I was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, may I ask you to carefully listen to the questions and to answer to what counsel asks you. If any further details are needed, they will certainly ask you. The question was: Did you at that time - and we're talking between the 22nd of April and the 22nd of June - whether you hold a certain duty in the 2nd army district, and if so, where? So just tell us what your duty was, where you fulfilled the duty. And if we'd like to know how you got there, whether the roads were bad or good, we'll certainly ask you or counsel will ask you. But we have to use our time as efficiently as possible, so please listen carefully and answer specifically to what you're asked. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, DP36, did you understand my question or should I repeat it? What duty did you hold, if you held any duty, as of the 22nd of April in the 2nd army district?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: When I arrived there, confusion reigned and I wasn't assigned to anything. I was merely with the department for morale and information. I was not issued with any document or hadn't been appointed to that duty in view of the events which ensued.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that you were not issued with an official document appointing you to a particular duty because of the disarray which ensued, can you tell us what were -- what was this disarray? What was this confusion which ensued after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: The command was blocked, and it was under constant fire from infantry weapons, from the 1st, 2nd, the 3rd, until the 3rd in the evening when we were captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, when you speak about the command, I believe -- I understood that you were talking about the command at Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when did you get to that command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, in the afternoon, in a military APC.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That 1st of May when you arrived in the command at Bistrik in an APC, did you already have information about the situation with regard to military facilities in the part of the city of Sarajevo, let me call it the centre proper of Sarajevo where there were some military facilities? I believe that is beyond dispute. Did you have any information as to the situation there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a lot of information. I didn't know much. It was only when I got there that I started finding out, because that was the beginning of the blockade of all the military facilities and establishments in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that it was the beginning of the blockade of all the military establishments in Sarajevo, did you personally see persons who were blocking those military institutions? Specifically, you were in the command at Bistrik, military. Did you have an opportunity to see the persons who had blocked that barracks, the barracks and specifically the command which you reached on the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: I could not see them on the 1st and 2nd of May because there was fire all the time. I saw them on the 3rd of May. On the 3rd of May, when they waylaid us and practically captured us. That was when I saw who that was. But those were different groups, well armed, however, very bold. And from what I knew, there had been an understanding which I am sure you are familiar with between the commander of the 2nd army district, General MacKenzie, and the leader of the Muslims, Izetbegovic, providing for our safe conduct. And I believe it was a gentleman's agreement. But, however, something happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, with the Chamber's leave we should like to show you a videotape which would be D348 exhibit. This is a tape which is about two minutes long.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, the Defence should like to show this tape. And then I will have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. May I ask the assistance of the technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we just get an indication, Mr. President, from the Defence which of the two tapes this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said number three, and I gave the transcript to your associate, and I believe that the interpreters' booths also have transcripts, but I can distribute more copies for the Chamber now and for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you, Mr. Usher, assist Ms. Pilipovic in distributing the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, since we're waiting for our engineers to start running the tape, I'll ask you some other questions. From what your -- from your answer, I gathered that you were captured on the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the video -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Around the building and in Vidova ulica it is peaceful there. No signs of fighting. The concentration of armed people from all sorts of leagues and berets is quite feasible at the corner of the street leading to Belgrade Hotel. That is exactly where the muzzles of their rifles and the cries to surrender are directed to. Surrender yourself! Further down the street towards the Belgrade hotel, the National Theatre and the Central Post Office there are a few JNA soldiers. Their vehicle is the only one that managed to pass the Skenderija crossroads but it failed to reach the JNA club building. The calls to surrender of the bullhorn are directed to them again. Surrender! Alongside the Sarajevo TV cameras there is the the omnipresent BBC and Martin Bell. With a smile on his face Dzevad Topic is inviting to attack the JNA centre and capture the men inside. Sniper rifles are repeatedly requested, and they are brought along with the Zoljas. On the street leading to the department store, explosives are laid and also bazookas are in position. Topic opens fire in the direction of the National Theatre and the Belgrade Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, can you tell us, concerning this footage that we just saw, can you tell me if you had an opportunity to see these men or similar men in such uniforms armed at the time when you were living -- that is, I'm referring to the 1st and 2nd of May and early 3rd May in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: This happened on the 2nd of May, and it was very dramatic. When a group of JNA soldiers were massacred and liquidated at Skenderija and another group was headed toward the JNA centre. I was present at this dramatic situation in the 2nd army district when they cut off the line for people who were seeking help with Motorolas, so they couldn't get any reinforcement and it happened on the 2nd of May. I did not personally see it but I know what the situation was in the 2nd army district and I knew that they could not be helped.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, as you were answering my questions, I believe you said that you were captured on the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were when you were captured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: I was in a column somewhere in the middle of the column, halfway through the column. And when the column started, suddenly fire was opened on us. It was hellish fire, so we all threw ourselves down on the ground. And they approached us, started disarming us, although we were ordered not to hold our weapons in a provocative position so that all our barrels were facing down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, can you tell us, in that column in which you were, who was leading that column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: At the head of the column was a UN vehicle which General MacKenzie, Colonel General Kukanjac, and the then-president of BH, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that they were in the column and you were captured and attacked, can you tell us who was it that attacked the column in which you were at the time of your capture? Did you, that is, learn which military formation was it? Was it army or ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Those were then Muslim paramilitary formations aligned in the Patriotic League. Then members of the Ministry of the Interior, and other groups led by certain criminals.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the Defence would like to show another tape, which is tape D312. There is a transcript. It is two minutes, and I think we could use the time before the break to see it so that tomorrow I could ask some questions about it. This is the footage which covers the events of the 3rd of May, referred to by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do not intend to put any questions to the witness, would it not be wiser to show it tomorrow so that he has it fresh in his mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has the interpretation now been restored?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, wise to put it -- but you can use the additional five minutes if you have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP36, when you said that on the 3rd May you were captured whilst in that column, can you tell us where were you as captives and how many people were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: Everybody was captured except the part of the column at the head, and certain killings also happened at that time. They brought us to the building of the physical culture centre in Sarajevo, and then I was singled out, I suppose because I had my navy insignia, with another woman and taken to the Evropa Hotel as a hostage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now when you answered this question, can you tell us if according to you this procedure -- this treatment of the column with which you were, that is, column which was leaving its facilities - and we are talking about members of the JNA - was that attack planned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36
utterances.text: That attack was perfectly planned. And to support my belief, there is a book by Sefer Halilovic, mastermind behind the Patriotic League and commander of the so-called BH army, and in his book he points out that they were the protagonists of the chaos and disarray, that is, the Patriotic League in Sarajevo of which everything that happened afterwards escalated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, since you remained in the territory of Sarajevo until the 22nd of June, do you have any direct knowledge whether the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew? And I mean both troops and the materiel from that territory. And if you know, when was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear that you are entering a -- more or less a new subject at this very moment. Looking at the clock, having only two or three minutes available, I'd prefer to deal with the documents of the previous witness first and ask this witness, DP36, to return tomorrow morning. Mr. DP36, we are close to where we adjourn until tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. I cannot promise you that we'll start at 9.00, because sometimes there are procedural issues to be dealt with, but we'd like to see you back in the same courtroom, tomorrow 9.00. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you are still about to give. Yes? Mr. Usher, would you then please pull the curtains down and escort the witness out of the courtroom. In the meanwhile, I'll ask the registrar to assist us with the documents of the previous witness and also to indicate where there seems to be a problem in the numbering of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1833, pseudonym sheet under seal; Exhibit D1834, map marked by witness; Exhibit D1835, set of three maps; Exhibit D1836, colour map marked by witness; Exhibit D938, letter from command of SRK dated 8 August 1993; D938.1, English translation; D1453, letter from SRK command dated 12 September 1992; Exhibit D1453.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to D1835, the set of three maps, the Prosecution has no objection to that exhibit being admitted into evidence. We would, however, ask that only those portions of that set of maps to which the witness referred be admissible, that is, that the witness testified about specific parts of that map and a very limited part of that map. We have no objection with respect to that portion of those maps, but with respect to the broader confrontation lines as depicted on that map, the Prosecution does object to consideration of those aspects to which the witness did not testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It might not be easy to cut out specifically those parts, but I do understand that there's no objection but that the Prosecution expresses that it does not accept those parts of the confrontation lines to be correctly drawn which have not been the subject of examination of the witness. I take it, Ms. Pilipovic, that specifically on those parts of the confrontation line the witness has testified about it, that's the reason why you tendered these documents into evidence and that we are not suggested to accept all of the other confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So being no argument with the parties on that aspect and hearing no objections, the documents are admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, was there not something about a number which was not clearly indicated on the -- in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I draw the attention of the parties to the fact that the Prosecution exhibit that had been re-used, and that is a photograph, P3750A, that it has not been correctly put in the transcript. It's the picture of the mosque and the minaret in a state of destruction. I just draw the attention to the parties of that so that it could -- that it would not create any confusion. We'll adjourn until -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Once again, we shall be referring to this exhibit again, so could we do the same thing as we did with the church at the time of Dobrinja; in other words, can we ask the Prosecution to let us know when was this photograph taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this information is available, please, Mr. Mundis, inform the Defence. And if that's -- if there would be any problem remaining, the Chamber will hear from you. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 1.49 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
